newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's southern rebels issue new demands.
newsitem.headline: Albania's southern rebels issue new demands.

text.p: Rebel leaders in southern Albania on Friday issued a fresh call for President Sali Berisha to resign but drew back from an earlier threat to set up a rival government.

Representatives of 14 rebel-held southern towns who have formed themselves into a National Committee of Public Salvation said they were ready to cooperate with the new interim national unity government under Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.

But they called for a voice in national political discussions and demanded that the government "neutralise" institutions helping Berisha remain in power, such as the state-run media and the Shik secret police.

Fino has drawn up a bill to reform the Shik, but this could be blocked in parliament by Berisha's Democratic Party, which controls 122 of the 140 seats in parliament following elections last May which were branded seriously flawed by foreign observers and boycotted by the opposition.

The rebels met in the southern town of Tepelene after Berisha ignored a Thursday deadline they set for him to quit. The embattled president says he will step down if his party loses elections scheduled for June.

The rebels also demanded fresh moves under the Finance Ministry to look into the scandal of shady pyramid investment schemes in which thousands of Albanians, particularly in the south, lost their savings. They called for an investigation into how the losses might be repaid.

The unrest sparked by the collapse of the pyramid schemes has left the army in chaos after much of its weaponry was looted by angry rebels and the country, Europe's poorest, badly in need of outside aid.
Greece said it was ready to help rebuild the Albanian army, but would need to study exactly what Albania needed before suggesting specific measures.
The European Union said it was prepared to send humanitarian aid "in two or three days", but stressed that military security must be ensured first.
The rebels had earlier threatened to set up a rival presidential council to challenge Berisha's authority in the south, which is ostensibly ruled by a loose network of citizens' councils.
In practice real control in many towns appears to be wielded by local mafias, all armed to the teeth with weapons looted from army barracks at the start of the uprising.

Albanian political party leaders, now part of the all-party government taking the country up to the June elections, have come out against using force to remove Berisha, saying the democratic process will decide.
In Tepelene, Salvation Committee member Latif Lato urged residents to observe the curfew and refrain from using their looted guns.
"Make no mistake, we have to fight against the same enemy, Sali Berisha. Let us help each other in order to better focus on him," Lato told reporters.
In Tirana the government, which controls the north and is seeking to reestablish control in the south, is locked in a power struggle with parliament, dominated by the Democrats.
Late on Thursday parliament voted down a draft bill submitted by Fino, of the ex-communist Socialist Party, to bring state television and radio under control of the government rather than parliament.
Fino argued that since the new government reflected all political shades it should take over control of the media for the time being, until the current crisis had been resolved.
However the speaker of parliament, Pjeter Arbnori, accused Fino of acting unconstitutionally, saying no previous government had ever tried to take over the media.
The parliament also blocked a government bill to lift press restrictions imposed under a state of emergency still in force.

Tirana airport remained open after the first flight for a week left for Sofia on Thursday. No civil flights were operating on Friday, but Austrian Airlines said it would resume flights to Tirana on Monday.
